passage:
Coaching note: investor update rehearsal.

Pankaj ran his slides for me on Tuesday evening. Slide 3 said "traction remains strong." When I asked what it meant, he admitted that two of the three big clients had paused orders. His voice dropped when he said it. He'd been dreading the call all week, and it showed in how much he had polished the story.

I asked him what the investor, Uma, would rather hear: a smooth story now, or a difficult number early enough to help. Pankaj thought about it for a while.

He rewrote slide 3 with the paused orders, the reasons he knew, and two questions for Uma about who could introduce him to new buyers. He asked her what she would do, not only whether she would fund him.

He may lose some investors' patience. But Pankaj looked less afraid when he left. Follow-up next Tuesday.

qa.q: What did slide 3 of Pankaj's deck originally say?
qa.a: Slide 3 said that traction remains strong.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj polish the story so much, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: Pankaj dreaded the investor call all week, and polishing the story was a way of softening bad news he was afraid to deliver.

qa.q: What change to the slide helped, and why?
qa.a: Adding the paused orders and asking for introductions turned a surprise into an honest update and invited Uma's advice as well as money.

qa.q: How might Uma react to hearing the bad news early?
qa.a: Uma may be disappointed about the paused orders, but hearing it early and directly makes it easier to trust Pankaj and to help.

grounding: Dreading an investor update, Pankaj polishes the story too much; a coach's note shows him giving honest bad news early and asking for advice.

passage:
It was 1 a.m. in the Andheri office, and Gautam was on his fifth draft of the investor update. Revenue had dropped for the second month. His draft said: "We are seeing an exciting period of repositioning."
Tejas, his co-founder, read it over his shoulder. "Repositioning? We lost two big clients."
Gautam's stomach churned. "If I say that, they'll panic."
"If we say that in six months, when the money's gone, they'll never trust us again."
Gautam stared at the screen. Then he deleted the paragraph and wrote: "Revenue fell 30% over two months after we lost two major clients. Here's what we've learned, and here's our plan. We'd value your advice on pricing and one intro to a logistics buyer."
He hit send at 2 a.m. By morning, two investors had replied with advice. One had not replied at all. Gautam decided that was a fair price for the truth.

qa.q: How far did revenue fall, according to the final update?
What was Gautam feeling as he wrote the first draft?
qa.a: He felt dread and anxiety, his stomach churning, afraid the investors would panic.

qa.q: What made the final update better?
qa.a: It gave the bad news honestly and early, explained the plan, and asked for advice and introductions, not only money.

qa.q: How might the investor who didn't reply see the update?
qa.a: That investor may be disappointed and pulling back, but Gautam accepts that some silence is the cost of honesty.

grounding: Dreading the investor update, the protagonist polishes the story, then gives honest bad news early and asks for advice, accepting some investors will go silent.

passage:
"Imran sir, before you read the update, can I tell you something?"
"Of course, Nazia. You sound nervous."
"I am. I wrote three versions. The first one made us sound fine. We're not."
"Go on."
"The school partnership in Lucknow fell through. We've lost a third of our users. We have five months of runway."
Imran was quiet for a moment. "Thank you for telling me now, not in December."
"I was scared you'd pull out."
"Some investors might. That's their choice. What do you need from me?"
"Advice, honestly. Should we focus on the coaching centres instead? And maybe an introduction to someone who's done that."
"That's a good question. I'll send you two names tonight."
Nazia let out a breath. "I thought this call would be the worst of my week."
"Surprises are the worst. This isn't a surprise anymore."

qa.q: How many months of runway did Nazia's startup have?
What was Nazia feeling before the call?
qa.a: Nazia felt nervous and scared that Imran would pull out after hearing the bad news.

qa.q: What did Nazia ask Imran for besides money?
qa.a: Advice on focusing on coaching centres and an introduction to someone who had done that.

qa.q: How does Imran see Nazia telling him early?
qa.a: He appreciates it and trusts Nazia more, since he values honest news now over a surprise in December.

grounding: Dreading the investor update, the protagonist chooses to share bad news early and ask for advice; the investor values the honesty over a later surprise.
